Draw from an approximate posterior

Source: R/sampling.R
sampling.Rd

Draws from the approximate joint posterior by a Gaussian copula: the skew-normal marginals of the fit are coupled through the correlation matrix \(R\) of the Laplace covariance. Each draw takes \(z \sim N(0, R)\), maps it to uniforms \(u_j = \Phi(z_j)\) and then to each parameter's skew-normal quantile, \(\vartheta_j = Q_j(u_j)\).

Usage

sampling(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'inla_vanilla'
sampling(object, nsamp = 1000L, fun = NULL, ...)

Arguments

object

An object to draw from.

...

For the inla_vanilla method, further arguments passed to fun. As in stats::optim(), a name that abbreviates nsamp or fun would be taken as that argument: a data argument named n would set the number of draws. Give such data a longer name, or wrap it in fun.

nsamp

Number of draws.

fun

Optional function applied to each draw. It receives one draw as a named numeric vector, like logpost, and returns a numeric vector of a fixed length (named, ideally). When NULL, the parameters themselves are returned.

Value

A numeric matrix with one row per draw: the parameters on the unconstrained scale, or the values of fun.

Details

For a fit with marginals = "gaussian" this is a draw from the joint Gaussian \(N(\tilde\vartheta, \Omega)\), centred at the VB mean (or at the mode when vb = FALSE).

Draws never call the log-posterior, so they are cheap: large nsamp costs little. Use fun for natural-scale or derived quantities, such as exp(log_sigma) or a covariance matrix built from several parameters.

Examples

set.seed(1)
y <- rnorm(30, mean = 5, sd = 2)
logpost <- function(theta, y) {
  sigma <- exp(theta[["log_sigma"]])
  sum(dnorm(y, theta[["mu"]], sigma, log = TRUE)) +
    dnorm(theta[["mu"]], 0, 10, log = TRUE) +
    dexp(sigma, log = TRUE) + theta[["log_sigma"]]
}
fit <- inla_vanilla(logpost, c(mu = 0, log_sigma = 0), y = y, silent = TRUE)

draws <- sampling(fit, nsamp = 2000)
head(draws)
#>            mu log_sigma
#> [1,] 5.603356 0.5173617
#> [2,] 5.125348 0.5495693
#> [3,] 5.285843 0.5657669
#> [4,] 5.141380 0.6024758
#> [5,] 4.707959 0.8346202
#> [6,] 5.023140 0.7795313

# A derived quantity: the coefficient of variation sigma / mu
cv <- sampling(fit, nsamp = 2000, fun = function(theta) {
  c(cv = exp(theta[["log_sigma"]]) / theta[["mu"]])
})
quantile(cv, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
#>      2.5%       50%     97.5% 
#> 0.2716513 0.3583291 0.4832763
